entries.summary: Coding agents can reach more than their task needs. See how Docker AI Governance controls network, filesystem, credential, and MCP access, then test it.
entries.text: You ask a coding agent to clean up one repository. If it has broad permissions, it may also reach your home directory, use your development credentials, and send requests to services you never approved. That gap between the task and the access you grant can turn a routine coding session into a data leak or lost work. In Sandboxing Claude and MCP, Hrittik walked through running Claude Code and an MCP server inside Docker Sandboxes using its command-line interface, sbx. That walkthrough started with outbound access blocked, allowed the endpoints needed for the task, and inspected requests to other destinations, including telemetry. The useful part was seeing an actual request fail at the network boundary. Now extend that workflow to a team. Models and providers will change, but the access rules still need to hold. A sandbox limits what an agent can reach on one machine. Organization governance adds shared rules, a managed way to run agents, and records of policy decisions. In this post, we’ll look at how one laptop can affect the whole organization, review two reported incidents, and connect them to four Docker controls: network policy, filesystem policy, managed credentials, and MCP access. Then we’ll test the network and filesystem controls with a simple bank administrator demo. How one laptop can affect the whole organization If an agent exposes a developer’s SSH key or cloud token, every system that accepts that credential may need investigation. entries.summary: Docker publishes fixed images for both Java4Shell and the NGINX HTTP/2 in the Docker Hardened Images (DHI) catalog.
entries.text: OpenJDK and Oracle disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) on November 17, and NGINX released fixes for two HTTP/2 flaws the next day. Docker began publishing fixed images for both in the Docker Hardened Images (DHI) catalog starting that same day. What we know about Java4Shell is that it’s a memory-corruption bug in the Java runtime that can let an attacker with no credentials run code inside a Java application. Many container images contain a Java runtime, including application images that bundle their own, so it affects teams well beyond the ones that write Java. Docker Hardened Images are the trusted foundation your applications should run on, because a flaw in the runtime inside an image is fixed only when that image is rebuilt, and Docker rebuilds its hardened images as soon as upstream fixes become available. Fixed images for the Amazon Corretto, SapMachine and Azul Zulu runtimes and for NGINX are in the catalog today, with Eclipse Temurin following as soon as Adoptium completes its fixed builds. TL;DR Affected: Java 17.0.6 and later, including Java 21, 25, 26 and 27, from every OpenJDK vendor. Only on some hardware: the bug is reachable only when the JVM runs on an x86-64 CPU with AVX-512 VBMI. The same image can be exposed on one host and not on another. Fixes are arriving vendor by vendor. Corretto, SapMachine and Zulu builds in DHI are fixed. Temurin, which many DHI application images use, is not released yet. Check the version the runtime reports. entries.summary: Docker launches a new brand built on trust. Learn why Docker is evolving for AI agents, what stays the same, and how to run agents securely with Docker.
entries.text: Evolving an iconic brand for the agentic era Today, Docker is officially launching its new brand, and I’m excited to tell you what it’s all about and why we think now is the time for change. Let’s start with the big picture. We’re living through a transformative moment: for Docker, for developers, for the industry, and quite possibly, for humanity itself. AI is creating possibilities that would have sounded like science fiction not long ago. But it’s also forcing the industry to confront an almost existential question: how do we harness all that power and intelligence without compromising security, governance, or control? Or, put more simply: how do we get to a point where we can actually trust agents? That one seemingly simple yet infinitely complex question is why we’re here today, introducing you to a new Docker. A new Docker, but a familiar story. We’ve been here before Ok, not exactly here, but once upon a time, a decade or so ago, the tech industry was at a similar inflection point. Digital transformation was the term du jour, promising a new way of engaging customers and powering the global economy. There was one big constraint, though: teams needed a better way to build, ship, and run software consistently across any environment. Enter a company you might have heard of: Docker. Together with all of you, Docker built the standard trusted by millions of developers. For over a decade, developers have relied on us to make software portable, open, reproducible, and secure.
entries.title: Meet the New Docker: Built to Run on Trust

entries.summary: Learn how Docker AI Governance secures agentic AI with sandbox policies, MCP tool governance, and audit visibility to support controlled AI agent workflows.
entries.text: The Agent Trust Gap The security problem changes once an AI agent can do more than answer a prompt. It can execute code, access files, connect to services, and call external tools. That creates a new security question for enterprises: how do you give an agent enough freedom to be useful without giving it more access than it actually needs? A model decision is not automatically an authorized action. That distinction becomes important the moment an agent can turn a model output into an action in a real system. The answer can’t rely only on the model. Agent behavior can vary, while security controls need to be clear and enforceable. That means putting controls around the environment where the agent runs, what it can access, which tools it can use, and what happens when a policy allows or blocks an action. For a CISO, this creates a trust gap. Approving the use of AI agents means being able to answer more than whether the model is capable: what access does the agent have, where are those boundaries enforced, and what evidence is available afterward? The goal is to let teams adopt agents without making model behavior itself the security boundary. Docker AI Governance approaches this through three areas: Sandbox Policies, MCP Tool Governance, and Audit + Visibility. Together, they address three practical questions security teams need answered: Where can the agent operate? What can it do? And can we see what happened? entries.summary: Give AI coding agents live web access with the Firecrawl kit for Docker Sandboxes. Learn to search, scrape, and crawl websites with network controls.
entries.text: Sandboxed agents cannot read the web A coding agent in Docker Sandboxes runs inside an isolated VM, the sandbox controls which hosts it can reach, and credentials stay on the host behind a proxy. The same controls keep the agent from opening a docs page, reading a changelog, or looking up an API that shipped after its training cutoff, so it writes code against the version it remembers. The usual fix is to widen the allowlist until the agent can fetch anything, which hands back most of what the sandbox took away. The Firecrawl kit gives the agent web search, page scraping, and site crawling through one added host, api.firecrawl.dev, and every page comes back as clean markdown. In this post, you’ll learn: How the Firecrawl sandbox kit plugs into a sandbox you already run How to install the sandbox kit and give your agent its first live-web task How to check that the SDK, the API key, and the network rule all work What the sandbox kit can’t do yet, and what new work it makes possible for your agent Why a kit The Firecrawl kit is a mixin (kind: mixin): it extends whichever workload you already run rather than defining a new sandbox. Its descriptor, firecrawl/firecrawl.yaml, declares four typed capabilities: An install step (lifecycle@1). It installs the Firecrawl Python SDK, firecrawl-py, pinned to 4.44.0, as the agent user, and fails sandbox creation if the install or import check fails. A credential (credential@1). entries.summary: A container shares the host kernel. Docker Sandboxes are microVMs with their own kernel and private Docker Engine. See how they differ and when to use each.
entries.text: If you’ve used Docker for a while, “Docker Sandboxes” might read as “a container with an AI agent inside.” Containers have been the unit of nearly everything Docker ships for over a decade, and a sandbox might sound like one more way to package a workload. They’re actually different technologies. A container is an isolated process that shares the host kernel with everything else on the machine. Docker Sandboxes are dedicated microVMs with their own Linux kernel, filesystem, network, and Docker Engine, built for autonomous coding agents that need a whole development machine to work in. A sandbox can run containers, which is part of why the two are easy to conflate. In his WeAreDevelopers keynote, Docker President Mark Cavage said containers are doing exactly the job they were designed to do, but we’re asking them to do a different job. Containers were built to isolate applications, which they still do well. But a coding agent is an actor: it makes decisions and operates on your systems the way a developer uses a laptop. It clones repositories, installs packages, starts databases, builds images, and tries again for hours. It can also act on instructions from files, web pages, and tool output that nobody reviewed. That different job needs a different boundary, and where that boundary sits determines how far an agent’s mistake can travel. entries.title: Docker Sandboxes vs. Containers: Choosing the Right Isolation for AI Agents

entries.summary: Docker partners with ActiveState to continue to provide one standard for trusted content across everything you and your teams build on.
entries.text: Trusted content is the foundation security-conscious organizations expect all builds to start from. Docker has made that possible for everyone by providing the foundation free. Docker Hardened Images (DHI) are open source under Apache 2.0, with a catalog of 4,000+ minimal images (and growing) built from source and continuously maintained by Docker. The catalog also carries customizable Helm charts and over 65,000 hardened system packages. For most services, adopting DHI is as simple as changing the FROM line. Teams building on a secure foundation now want the same assurance for the open source their applications install. That open source is a different layer of the supply chain, where thousands of upstream projects are pulled in at build time by pip, npm and Maven, and by coding agents as well. Docker is committed to one standard for trusted content across everything teams build on. A new partnership with ActiveState, the company that has been securing open source since 1997, extends that standard to the packages themselves. Together, we give teams the same assurance on both layers, from the hardened images Docker maintains to the packages developers and their agents install on them. Once configured, the integration allows developers and AI coding assistants to continue using familiar package managers and development workflows, while approved dependencies are sourced through governed repositories rather than directly from public registries. entries.summary: See how CNCF Score improved container security with Docker Scout, Hardened Images, and the Docker-Sponsored Open Source Program.
entries.text: Score, a CNCF Sandbox project, recently joined the Docker-Sponsored Open Source (DSOS) Program to strengthen the security of its container images and release pipeline. In this post, the Score maintainers share what we adopted (Docker Hub, Docker Scout, Docker Hardened Images, the Docker GitHub Builder, and OIDC connections), the results we measured, and how other open source projects, within the CNCF and beyond, can apply the same practices by default. The Opportunity In September 2025, the CNCF announced a partnership with Docker to expand infrastructure support for project maintainers through the Docker-Sponsored Open Source (DSOS) Program. The partnership gives CNCF projects access to Docker’s security scanning tools, container registry, and best-practice resources at no cost. This aligned closely with the discussions held at the Maintainer Summit NA 2025 in Atlanta, which centered on increasing collaboration across CNCF projects and demonstrating security best practices. The Docker-Sponsored Open Source (DSOS) Program supports non-commercial open source projects with Docker tooling and infrastructure. Eligible projects receive: Verified Docker-Sponsored Open Source badge Removal of rate limits for developers Access to Docker Scout for software supply chain management Insights and analytics Repository logo Improved discoverability on Docker Hub Docker Hub Before: Score publishes different container images: the CLIs of score-compose, score-k8s, score-helm and score-radius;
entries.title: CNCF Score project improved its security posture by joining the Docker-Sponsored Open Source Program

entries.summary: Docker is a founding member of the Blueprint Alliance, a 12-company reference architecture for securing AI agents, built around four governance questions.
entries.text: In 2025, the average global Fortune 500 enterprise had fewer than 15 AI agents in use. Gartner expects that number to explode to more than 150,000 by 2028. Only 13 percent of organizations think they have the right governance for today, and AI is evolving and moving faster than any other technology paradigm in our history. Today, most security leaders face an agentic Sophie’s choice: allow AI adoption without the right controls and hope for the best, or block it and become the obstacle to a priority the business has already set (while adoption continues in the shadows, anyway). But there is a third option, one in which organizations fully tap into the transformative power of agentic agents without having to live in fear of a catastrophic security failure. The good news is history has already shown how to get there. How technology gets adopted Historically, technology adoption has followed a reliable pattern. A capability spreads, each vendor and team builds its own approach, the inconsistency becomes expensive and ineffective, leading the industry to agree to a shared baseline. Adoption then accelerates. Take the credit card industry, for example. The big credit brands each ran their own security programs, and merchants had to satisfy every one. This was, of course, cumbersome for the vendors, but also for the customers, too. entries.title: The Ecosystem is the Answer: Docker, the Blueprint Alliance, and the Importance of Collaboration in the Agentic Era

entries.summary: Docker Sandboxes support three ways to organize an agent’s code: shared mounts, Git worktrees, and clone mode. Here’s how to choose between them.
entries.text: Giving an agent a sandbox also means deciding which files it will work on. You can share a checkout from your host, give it a separate working directory for a task, or keep the repository entirely inside the sandbox. Each arrangement changes how you, the human, participate in the work. You might want to watch the diff in your local editor and make changes alongside the agent, or give it room to manage several tasks while you review the results. sbx supports both. The way you organize the checkout can change as you ask the agent to take on more of the work. Mounting a repository from your host Sharing a checkout puts the agent in the working tree you already use. Run sbx run from your project directory, and it mounts that directory at the same absolute path inside the sandbox: $ cd ~/my-project $ sbx run claude Open a file in your local editor while the agent works on it, and you’ll see changes as they happen. Git works from either side, so you choose whether you want to let the agent make commits or you do it yourself. Development servers on your host can pick up the edits through hot reload, using the runtime and dependencies installed on your host. This fits close collaboration on one task. The coordination cost comes from sharing that working tree: switching branches changes the files the agent sees, and your edits become part of its ongoing work.
